title: "Lecture 9: Interest-Rate Futures"
subtitle: "Translate rate views into liquid, margined exposure"
author: "BUS 411"

## Futures change exposure without moving the cash portfolio

> A futures contract separates **interest-rate exposure** from ownership of the underlying bond.

- Hedge duration quickly
- Express a rate or curve view
- Create synthetic exposure
- Preserve liquidity in the cash portfolio

## The clearinghouse makes the contract tradable

| Long futures | Clearinghouse | Short futures |
|---|---|---|
| Commits to buy | Guarantees performance | Commits to sell |
| Gains when price rises | Marks positions daily | Gains when price falls |

Most positions are closed with an offsetting trade before delivery.

## Bond futures translate price direction into rate direction

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Long futures

- Price rises → gain
- Rates usually fall
- Adds positive duration
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Short futures

- Price falls → gain
- Rates usually rise
- Removes duration
:::
:::

## Margin is collateral—not the purchase price

- **Initial margin:** posted when the position opens
- **Maintenance margin:** minimum account balance
- **Variation margin:** restores the account after losses
- **Marking to market:** converts each day's price move into cash

Notional value measures exposure; margin measures performance collateral.

## Daily settlement changes cash-flow timing

One Treasury futures contract is long at 100-00. One point is worth \$1,000.

| Day | Settlement | Daily cash flow |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 100-00 | — |
| 1 | 100-12 | +\$375 |
| 2 | 99-28 | −\$500 |
| 3 | 100-08 | +\$375 |

$$\text{Cumulative gain}=375-500+375=\$250$$

## Futures trade standardization for liquidity

| Feature | Futures | Forwards |
|---|---|---|
| Venue | Exchange | Over the counter |
| Terms | Standardized | Customized |
| Credit support | Clearinghouse and margin | Bilateral agreement |
| Settlement | Daily | Usually at maturity |
| Exit | Offset readily | Negotiate or unwind |

Customization and liquidity pull in opposite directions.

## The underlying determines the rate exposure

| Contract family | Primary exposure |
|---|---|
| SOFR futures | Forward overnight financing rate |
| Fed Funds futures | Average effective policy rate |
| Treasury futures | Price of a deliverable Treasury basket |

Contract selection begins by locating the risk on the curve.

Eurodollar futures historically referenced 3-month LIBOR; SOFR futures now provide the main exchange-traded USD short-rate exposure after the LIBOR transition.

## SOFR futures quote a rate as an index

$$\text{Futures price}=100-\text{implied SOFR rate}$$

A price of 95.25 implies:

$$100-95.25=4.75\%$$

For a Three-Month SOFR contract, a one-basis-point move is approximately:

$$\$1{,}000{,}000(0.0001)\left(\frac{90}{360}\right)=\$25$$

## A long SOFR future benefits when the implied rate falls

Price moves from 95.25 to 95.40:

$$\Delta \text{price}=+15\text{ bps}$$

$$\text{Gain to long}=15(\$25)=\$375$$

The implied rate falls from 4.75% to 4.60%.

<div class="takeaway">SOFR futures prices and implied rates move in opposite directions.</div>

## Fed Funds futures focus on the policy month

- Reference the average effective federal funds rate for a calendar month
- Help infer the market-implied policy path
- Blend expectations with risk premiums and contract conventions

An implied rate is a hedgeable market price—not a guaranteed forecast.

## Treasury futures deliver a basket, not one named bond

- Contract specifies maturity and eligibility rules
- Short chooses an eligible issue for delivery
- Long pays the invoice amount
- Delivery flexibility has economic value

The futures contract inherits risk from the bond expected to be delivered.

## Treasury prices use points and 32nds

$$107\text{-}16=107+\frac{16}{32}=107.50$$

For \$100,000 face value:

$$107.50\%\times \$100{,}000=\$107{,}500$$

A one-tick move of $1/32$ is worth \$31.25 per \$100,000 contract.

## Conversion factors normalize different deliverable bonds

When futures price is quoted per \$100 par, the invoice amount is:

$$\text{Invoice}=\frac{\text{Futures price}}{100}\times\text{conversion factor}\times\text{face value}+\text{accrued interest}$$

Conversion factors make different coupons and maturities comparable—but do not make delivery economics identical.

## The cheapest-to-deliver bond minimizes net delivery cost

$$
\text{Net delivery cost}
=\text{Cash bond price}-\text{Futures price}\times\text{CF}
$$

| Bond | Cash price | CF | Futures × CF | Net cost |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 118.00 | 1.120 | 112.00 | 6.00 |
| B | 104.50 | 0.995 | 99.50 | **5.00** |

Bond B is cheapest to deliver even though delivery compares adjusted—not raw—prices.

## Cash-and-carry links futures and cash prices

For a simple asset with price $P$, financing rate $r$, income yield $c$, and horizon $t$:

$$F=P[1+t(r-c)]$$

- Financing cost raises fair futures value
- Coupon income lowers fair futures value
- Arbitrage pressures large deviations toward fair value

## Carry can place futures above or below cash

Suppose $P=100$, $r=7\%$, $c=5\%$, and $t=0.5$:

$$F=100[1+0.5(0.07-0.05)]=101$$

- If market futures = 103: buy cash and sell futures
- If market futures = 99: short cash and buy futures

Real trades also include coupons, repo, bid-ask costs, and delivery choices.

## Delivery options break the one-bond pricing shortcut

The short may have flexibility over:

- **quality:** which eligible bond to deliver;
- **timing:** when to deliver within the delivery month;
- **wild card:** whether to act after the futures settlement is set.

These options generally benefit the short and reduce the futures price.

## Duration management starts with the target exposure

1. Measure current portfolio duration or DV01.
2. Define the target exposure.
3. Identify the relevant futures contract and CTD.
4. Estimate futures DV01.
5. Trade, monitor, and rebalance.

The hedge ratio is an exposure equation—not a forecast.

## Futures DV01 comes from the CTD bond

Approximate CTD DV01:

$$\text{DV01}_{CTD}=D_{mod}\times MV\times 0.0001$$

Approximate futures DV01:

$$\text{DV01}_{fut}\approx\frac{\text{DV01}_{CTD}}{\text{conversion factor}}$$

The estimate changes if the cheapest-to-deliver bond changes.

## Hedge contracts equal the DV01 gap divided by futures DV01

Portfolio DV01 is \$27,840. CTD data: duration 6.5, price 98.50, face \$100,000, conversion factor 0.9200.

$$\text{DV01}_{CTD}=6.5(98{,}500)(0.0001)=\$64.03$$

$$\text{DV01}_{fut}=64.03/0.9200=\$69.59$$

$$N=27{,}840/69.59\approx400\text{ contracts}$$

A long cash portfolio sells futures to reduce DV01.

## A perfect DV01 match is still an imperfect hedge

- CTD can switch
- Cash and futures yields may not move equally
- Credit spreads can move independently of Treasury rates
- Curve shifts may be nonparallel
- Contract quantity must be rounded
- Margin creates liquidity needs

Hedge effectiveness must be monitored after the trade.

## Curve trades require maturity-specific contracts

| View | Possible structure |
|---|---|
| Rates rise broadly | Short Treasury futures |
| Curve steepens | Short long-maturity / long short-maturity futures |
| Front-end cuts arrive sooner | Long selected SOFR futures |

DV01 weighting helps isolate slope from an unintended level position.

The same exposure logic can create a **synthetic bond allocation**: hold liquid collateral and add the desired rate exposure with futures. Shifting futures positions can also change the bond-versus-equity allocation without immediately trading the underlying portfolios.

## A practical futures decision has four layers

1. **Exposure:** What rate, maturity, and direction matter?
2. **Instrument:** Which contract maps most closely to that risk?
3. **Sizing:** What DV01 or tick-value hedge ratio is required?
4. **Implementation:** What can CTD, basis, margin, and liquidity do to the result?

## Futures are precise tools only when the mapping is precise

- Futures provide liquid, leveraged rate exposure.
- Daily margining controls credit risk but creates cash-flow demands.
- SOFR prices move opposite implied forward rates.
- Treasury futures depend on conversion factors and delivery options.
- DV01 sizing is the starting point; basis risk determines realized hedge quality.
